documents: Antony et al. 2022, Weather and Climate Extremes 35, 100409 (published PDF, 12 pages)
Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): abstract and figure/table captions only
pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) for the abstract (§0 ¶1) and captions (Fig. N, as printed); the XML text contains no body paragraphs, so body-text steps cite printed journal pages, which equal PDF pages counted from 1 (p. N)

entry.evidence: The authors name a literature gap: surge studies in the Red Sea are few and local, and 'a basin-wide analysis of surges is still lacking'; [...]

sequences.source_document: Antony et al. 2022, published PDF (body) and publisher XML text (abstract, captions)

steps.action: States the gap (no basin-wide surge analysis) and sets the aims: a validated long-term meteorological sea-level hindcast and a description of the extremes.
steps.quote: Our study aims at addressing this gap

steps.action: Takes from Churchill et al. (2018) that weather-band sea-level variations are basin-coherent and associated with southern Red Sea winds.
steps.quote: the weather-band signals are associated with winds over the southern Red Sea

steps.action: Builds a depth-averaged ADCIRC model on an unstructured mesh (~500 m at the coast, GEBCO bathymetry, uniform quadratic friction, no tidal forcing) forced hourly by 5 km assimilative WRF winds and pressure, run in 1-year blocks for 1980–2016.
steps.quote: We implemented the ADvanced CIRCulation (ADCIRC) model

steps.action: Obtains three years of hourly tide-gauge records at six Saudi coast stations and de-tides them with TASK-2000 (61 constituents, Sa and Ssa excluded) to get residual sea level.
steps.quote: three years (2013–2015) of hourly sea-level observations from six tide gauges

steps.action: Compares modeled and observed residual sea level visually and finds a seasonal mismatch, because the barotropic model omits steric and mass-exchange effects.
steps.quote: An initial visual comparison of the two time series suggested this issue.

steps.action: Applies a 30-day Butterworth high-pass filter to both series and re-compares them with RMSE, correlation, scatter and q-q plots (mean r 0.75, RMSE 0.05 m); positive extremes are slightly overestimated and negative extremes underestimated.
steps.quote: we de-seasoned both the modeled and observed data using a Butterworth high-pass filter

steps.action: Attributes the remaining model-data mismatches to mesoscale eddies the model cannot reproduce, and keeps the model.
steps.quote: These could be related to mesoscale eddies

steps.action: Restricts the hindcast's validated scope to positive (high) sea-level extremes.
steps.quote: the model hindcast is relevant to examine the variability of the positive (high) sea-level extremes

steps.action: Characterizes observed residual sea level: an annual cycle of 0.12–0.15 m, inter-station correlations above 0.89 (Table 1), similar standard deviations, and wavelet power in the 3–100 d band that is stronger in January–March.
steps.quote: The residual sea-level time series plotted in Fig. 3 show a remarkable uniformity across the stations.

steps.action: Composites WRF wind and pressure 24 h before 7 high and 15 low winter extremes: SSE winds and low pressure over the southern Red Sea during highs, NNW winds and high pressure during lows.
steps.quote: strong south-southeast (SSE) wind field (wind speeds up to 14 m/s) over the southern Red Sea

steps.action: Maps band-passed correlations of basin-averaged sea level with wind components and pressure: about 0.7 with meridional wind over the southern Red Sea, about -0.6 with zonal wind, -0.3 to -0.5 with pressure.
steps.quote: highest positive correlations (about 0.7) between basin-averaged sea level and the meridional component of surface winds

steps.action: Checks the 24 h wind-to-sea-level lag against the individual gauges (22–25 h) and confirms common 3–100 d power with a cross-wavelet spectrum (Fig. 7).
steps.quote: consistent with the individual tide gauge time series (22–25 h)

steps.action: Maps maximum, minimum and mean meteorological sea level over 1980–2016 from the hindcast at each grid point (Fig. 8): about 0.85 m in the northern Gulf of Suez, 0.3–0.5 m elsewhere.
steps.quote: The maximum sea levels toward the northern end of the Gulf reach approximately 0.85 m

steps.action: Derives the mean seasonal cycle of monthly maxima with the Dangendorf et al. (2012) detrend-and-average method: amplitudes 0.06–0.16 m, peak in winter (Fig. 9).
steps.quote: Sea-level extremes are frequent from January to March.

steps.action: Runs pressure-only, wind-only and combined forcing simulations over 5 years from 2009 to separate the two meteorological drivers.
steps.quote: performing model simulations only accounting for each individual forcing separately

steps.action: Compares the maxima and time series of the separate-forcing runs with the combined run (Fig. 10): wind dominates, with a weak nonlinear interaction.
steps.quote: suggesting that the pressure contribution is one order of magnitude less than the wind contribution

steps.action: Tests annual maxima (June–May years) at each grid point for monotonic trend with Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope (Fig. 11); rates of ±1 mm/yr are not significant at α = 0.1.
steps.quote: these rates are not statistically significant (at significance α = 0.1)

steps.action: Repeats the trend test on the 99th and 95th percentiles and the mean (figures not shown) and on extremes of the meteorological forcing fields; no significant trends.
steps.quote: [...] 95th percentiles and mean regime of the meteorological sea level do not suggest any significant trends

steps.action: Sets the wind-driver finding beside Churchill et al. (2018) and finds agreement on the role of SSE winds over the southern Red Sea.
steps.quote: We also note the important role of SSE winds over the southern Red Sea

steps.action: Uses textbook wind setup (proportional to wind speed, inversely to depth) and the inverse barometer effect to frame the expected responses.
steps.quote: This sea-level change is directly proportional to the wind speed and inversely proportional to the water depth

steps.action: Keeps the explanation: SSE winds produce setup and NNW winds setdown, low pressure adds to highs, and Gulf of Suez shallowness and geometry give the largest values.
steps.quote: the SSE winds over the southern Red Sea generate a setup while during low sea-level events, the NNW winds create a setdown

steps.action: Sets the no-trend result beside Shanas et al. (2017), who found no trends in winds and waves, and Mawdsley and Haigh (2016), who found no surge trends at most global gauges.
steps.quote: consistent with the results of Shanas et al. (2017)

steps.action: Keeps the hindcast climatology: maxima of 0.30–0.50 m in the basin and 0.85 m in the Gulf of Suez, frequent in January–March, wind-dominated, with no significant trend over 1980–2016.
steps.quote: with the highest values (0.85 m) in the Gulf of Suez

tree.answer: Meteorological sea-level extremes (surges) in the Red Sea
Only partly: six gauges for 3 years; a 37-year hindcast is needed
Estimate and describe the basin-wide climatology of extremes
No rival explanations; the two forcings (wind and pressure) are apportioned
Separate-forcing runs give different maxima (wind 0.2–0.3 m, pressure 0.1–0.2 m)
Conditions found (weather events), set only inside the model

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: 37 winters and repeated events give the seasonal cycle and trend tests
Survives filtered tide-gauge validation and trend checks on several statistics
Kept: estimates of maxima, seasonality and no trend

end.claim: A validated (r about 0.75, RMSE about 0.05 m) 37-year hindcast shows wind-driven meteorological sea-level maxima of about 0.30–0.50 m in the Red Sea and 0.85 m in the Gulf of Suez, frequent in January–March, with no significant trend over 1980–2016.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the 37-year, ~500 m ADCIRC hindcast forced by downscaled WRF fields there would be no basin-wide map of extremes, seasonal cycle or trend; the tide gauges cover only three years at six eastern stations.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition: the hindcast was built to fill a gap and the tide-gauge data were pre-existing (p. 2–3). The model faced a validation it could have failed (p. 4), and the forcing and trend tests could have come out otherwise (p. 7). But the headline maxima (0.85 m, Gulf of Suez) were never compared with local observations. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen: the filter was chosen after an initial visual comparison (p. 4).

imports.item: Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen's slope estimator
Morlet wavelet and cross-wavelet analysis (via Grinsted et al. 2004)

novelty_claims.quote: a basin-wide analysis of surges is still lacking
Sea-level extremes of meteorological origin have been little explored in the Red Sea.

limits: The XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite printed/PDF pages. No review file was supplied, so there is no review sequence. Validation uses three years at six eastern (Saudi) gauges. None lies in the Gulf of Suez, so the headline 0.85 m maximum is not checked against local data (inference). No uncertainty is attached to the mapped maxima; the resolution is inferred from the gauge RMSE. WRF forcing skill is taken from the authors' own and others' earlier studies, not checked here. Tide-surge interaction and mesoscale eddies are left out (eddies deferred to future 3D work, p. 10). The wind/pressure apportionment covers only 5 years. Percentile trend figures are not shown. Sub-claims: wind-driven origin is best_explanation (correlations, composites, forcing runs; no rival stated); winter seasonality is regularity_in_range (1980–2016); the no-trend result is estimate_with_resolution at α = 0.1. Composition none_fits: a problem-driven descriptive hindcast with no rivals. It is nearest to natures_repetition (seasonal regularity and trend across 37 winters), but the main products are model-based estimates, not a fitted regularity.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Numerical hindcast (ADCIRC forced by WRF) as the long-term data source
alternatives_considered.reason: Long-term tide-gauge observations are very scarce in the Red Sea
The Red Sea has a low tidal regime and the interaction effects are expected to be small

alternatives_considered.chosen: De-tiding with 61 constituents, excluding Sa and Ssa
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Including the seasonal harmonics Sa and Ssa
alternatives_considered.reason: These are mostly non-tidal (meteorological and oceanographic) in origin

alternatives_considered.chosen: Comparison after a 30-day Butterworth high-pass filter
alternatives_considered.reason: The barotropic model does not account for seasonal steric and mass-exchange effects

alternatives_considered.chosen: Lag estimated on the basin-averaged sea level
alternatives_considered.reason: Uniformity of residual sea levels across stations

alternatives_considered.chosen: June–May years for annual maxima and percentiles
alternatives_considered.reason: To avoid splitting the winter extreme season between adjacent years
